claims.text: Prolonged mechanical loading at elevated temperature causes localized short-range ordering in a nominally single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Prolonged mechanical loading at elevated temperature causes partial phase transformations in the alloy.
Localized short-range ordering impedes dislocation motion by increasing activation barriers and lattice friction.
Restricted dislocation motion creates localized stress concentrations.
The resulting stress concentrations trigger a tough-to-brittle transition.
The initial alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has high ductility under ambient conditions.
The initial alloy has high fracture toughness under ambient conditions.
In-situ mechanical loading over varied temperatures and strain rates can track the emergence of ordering, faults, or microtwins.
Temperatures of 600–800 °C and moderate-to-high strain rates are representative of demanding engineering service.
Ordering-induced slip barriers restrict dislocation flow.
Restricted dislocation flow amplifies local stress and favors crack nucleation and propagation.
Elevated-temperature loading will cause a measurable decrease in fracture toughness relative to the initially ductile baseline.
Brittle cracking will coincide with observable short-range ordering or emerging secondary defect structures.
Single-phase CrMnFeCoNi alloys have high fracture toughness at room temperature.
The proposed embrittlement occurs primarily at 600–800 °C and/or at strain rates typical of accelerated testing.
The timescale of ordering or transformation and its dependence on composition and stress–temperature gradients are insufficiently established.
Failure to observe ordering or phase transformation together with failure to observe toughness loss or brittle-crack initiation under the stated conditions would invalidate the hypothesis.
